Similar to how [[inertia]] describes the tendency of an object or system to resist changes to its motion, '''moment of inertia''' $I_{\Delta}(S)$ describes the tendency of an object or system $(S)$ to resist changes '''specifically''' to its rotational motion about axis $\Delta$.

By definition,

{{#content:Q2049}}

[[File:Moment-of-inertia.svg|center|500px]]

<blockquote>
Denote the position of the unit mass $dm$ as $M$, then $\vec r_m =\overrightarrow{OM} \Rightarrow \vec r_m \wedge \Delta=\overrightarrow{HM}$, where $H \in \Delta \land \overrightarrow{HM}\bot \Delta$. i.e., $\left\| \vec r_m \wedge \Delta \right\|$ measures the vertical distance from $M$ to $\Delta$ $d(M)$.
</blockquote>

== Orthogonal base ==

In an [[Orthonormality#Orthonormal_basis|orthonormal basis]], it can be derived that:

$$
\begin{cases}
I_{Ox}(S)=\int_S(y^2+z^2)\,dm\\
I_{Oy}(S)=\int_S(x^2+z^2)\,dm\\
I_{Oz}(S)=\int_S(x^2+y^2)\,dm
\end{cases}
$$

And it is thereby abstracted a combined moment of inertia according to the origin $O$:

$$
I_O=\int_S(x^2+y^2+z^2)\,dm
$$

which estimates the general tendency of $(S)$ to resist an arbitrary rotation around $O$.
